title: Fret Board
primary_metric: cents of pitch deviation from true equal temperament at the 12th fret

options.A: Mark every fret using the Precision Method — the exact twelfth-root-of-two ratio, calculated to four decimal places at each fret
options.B: Mark every fret using the Rule of Eighteen — the traditional whole-number-divisor shortcut

sources.claim: Exact formula for fret distance from the nut under equal temperament, and the numeric value of the twelfth root of two
sources.value: distance(n) = L x [1 - (1/2)^(n/12)]; twelfth root of two ~= 1.0594630943593
sources.title: Calculating Fret Positions
sources.note: Standard equal-temperament fret formula, algebraically equivalent to the iterative StewMac form. No publication date on the source page; graded HIGH because the figure is a fixed mathematical definition, not a claim that could go stale.

sources.claim: The modern, more precise fret-spacing divisor (17.817154) some shops use instead of the traditional 18
sources.title: Fret Scale Rule Instructions
sources.note: Used only as contextual background in Appendix C (explaining that the shop's own 'rule of 18' shortcut is a rounding of this more precise constant) -- NOT the divisor used to compute Appendix C's own table, which correctly models the historical whole-number rule of 18 per S3.

sources.claim: The traditional 'rule of 18' historically used an exact whole-number divisor of 18, and produces frets that trend flat of true equal temperament
sources.title: Was the Rule of 18 Good Enough?
sources.note: Confirms the divisor is exactly 18 in the traditional method (not a rounding of 17.817 in the source itself), and that the resulting frets trend flat of true equal temperament -- both facts used in Appendix C/D. The article does not give an exact cents figure at fret 12; that figure is derived (see below), consistent with this source's qualitative finding.

sources.claim: Named standard guitar scale lengths and typical modern-electric fret-count range
sources.value: Fender-style 25.5 in; Gibson-style 24.75 in; PRS-style 25 in; 21-24 frets typical for modern electric guitars
sources.title: Guitar Scale Length Explained
sources.note: Scale length (25.5 in, Fender-style) is used directly as this build's spec. Fret-count range (21-24) is used only as the basis for Modeling Assumption MA2, not as a directly-claimed figure, since the exact count for THIS build is a scenario choice.

deliverables.text: A fret-position table, Precision Method: distance from the nut for frets 1-12 using the twelfth-root-of-two ratio, to four decimal places.
A fret-position table, Rule of Eighteen: distance from the nut for frets 1-12 using the traditional whole-number-divisor shortcut.
A cents-of-deviation conversion at fret 12, using the D1/D2 length difference and the cents formula in Appendix D.
A GCF string-length-ratio table for frets 1-5, reduced to lowest terms, identifying which frets land on simple whole-number ratios.
A recommendation comparing both methods' 12th-fret deviation against the acceptable intonation tolerance and the re-fret cost.

balance.argument_a: The Precision Method is exact by construction — at fret 12 it lands exactly at half the scale length, matching true equal temperament with zero drift. A shop that wants clean intonation across the whole neck, including upper frets, has a hard case for A regardless of extra bench time.
balance.argument_b: The Rule of Eighteen is faster to mark, requires no calculator precision, and is the method generations of working luthiers actually used on instruments that intonated well enough to play professionally. If its cents-of-deviation at fret 12 sits inside the acceptable tolerance, the Precision Method's extra time buys accuracy nobody can hear, against a real five-day deadline.
balance.margin_basis: Compare the 12th-fret cents-of-deviation figure (Appendix D, computed from the Appendix B vs. Appendix C length difference) against the acceptable intonation tolerance in cents (Appendix D) once both are sourced or stated as a Modeling Assumption in case-research.
balance.margin_note: The primary metric (cents of deviation at fret 12) is a one-sided error metric, not a total each option accrues -- the Precision Method is ~0 cents by construction, and the derived Rule of Eighteen figure is ~12.5 cents flat (see Appendix D), which is a ~2.5x overshoot of the stated MA1 tolerance (5 cents), not a SPEC §2-style close percentage race. This was flagged as a genuine open question for case-qa/case-readiness to weigh, not resolved here: the concept sheet (C4) declared 'Sensitivity: None' and 'Split risk: NONE' and scored this case for its domain-opening value rather than a tight balance, but a hard ~2.5x miss on the primary metric alone is a legitimate SPEC §2 balance concern a human should look at before this case reaches case-qa. The case's real defensibility, per FACILITATOR.md, rests on cost/deadline/historical-precedent arguments for B rather than the primary metric alone -- worth an explicit balance re-check, not a silent pass.

modeling_assumptions.text: Acceptable intonation tolerance a professional luthier targets, at the 12th fret
modeling_assumptions.basis: No single published professional trade standard states one hard number. Guitar-technician/luthier discussion threads converge on a working range of roughly 2-6 cents, and published psychoacoustic pitch-discrimination research places the just-noticeable difference for most listeners in a similar few-cents range. 5 cents sits inside that commonly cited range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The case's answer is sensitive to this value (Rule of Eighteen's derived ~12.5-cent deviation at fret 12 sits outside this stated tolerance); the case does not print the resulting verdict here, per case-write SKILL.md's rule against stating the answer key in a Sensitivity/Why column.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Falls inside the 21-24 fret range StewMac (S4) states is typical for a modern electric guitar; the exact count for this build is a shop/client choice, not itself a published standard.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low -- does not change the per-fret math in D1-D4.
